questions.subject: en
questions.passage: Last summer Aysel got her first part-time job at a small café near her school. At first she found it difficult. She had to remember dozens of orders, and once she dropped a whole tray of glasses in front of the customers. She wanted to quit after the first week, but the owner, Mr Kamal, told her that everyone makes mistakes at the beginning. He taught her to write orders down and to carry fewer things at once. By the end of the summer, Aysel was one of the fastest waiters in the café. She says the job taught her more about responsibility than any lesson at school, and she used the money she earned to buy a laptop for her studies.
questions.text: Where did Aysel work last summer?
options: at a café near her school

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: Every year millions of tonnes of plastic end up in the world's oceans. Most of it comes from land: bottles, bags and packaging are carried by rivers or blown by the wind into the sea. Plastic does not disappear; instead, it slowly breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics. Sea animals often mistake these pieces for food. Turtles, for example, sometimes eat plastic bags because they look like jellyfish. Some countries have banned single-use bags, and many beaches are now cleaned by volunteers. However, scientists say that the most effective solution is to produce and use less plastic in the first place.
questions.text: Where does most ocean plastic come from?

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: When Elvin was helping his grandfather clean the attic, he found an old wooden box. Inside there was a map of their village, drawn by hand more than sixty years ago. On the map, a small cross was marked next to the old mill. Elvin was sure it was hidden treasure. The next morning he and his sister walked to the mill with a shovel. After an hour of digging, they found a metal tin. There was no gold inside — only a letter and a black-and-white photo of a young man. The young man was their grandfather. In the letter, he had written about his dreams for the future. That evening the whole family read the letter together, and grandfather laughed until he cried.
questions.text: Where did Elvin find the box?

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: Every Thursday afternoon a group of teenagers meets at the local community centre to teach older people how to use smartphones. The idea came from Leyla, a sixteen-year-old student, after her grandmother asked her for help with video calls for the tenth time. Now about fifteen pensioners come to each session. They learn how to send messages, take photos and pay bills online. The volunteers say patience is the most important skill. 'We explain the same thing many times, and that's fine,' says Leyla. The older learners, in return, share stories about their lives. Several of them have become good friends with the students.
questions.text: When do the sessions take place?

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: Honeybees are famous for making honey, but their most important job is pollination. When a bee visits a flower to collect nectar, tiny grains of pollen stick to its body. As it flies from flower to flower, it carries this pollen with it, which helps plants produce fruit and seeds. Many of the fruits and vegetables we eat depend on this process. Unfortunately, bee populations have fallen in many parts of the world. Scientists believe the main reasons are the use of certain pesticides, the loss of wild flowers and disease. Planting flowers in gardens and on balconies is one simple way that ordinary people can help bees.
questions.text: What is the bees' most important job, according to the text?

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: Since the pandemic, online learning has become a normal part of education. Supporters say it gives students freedom: they can watch lessons again, study at their own speed and learn from teachers in other cities or even other countries. Critics, however, point out that not every family has a fast internet connection or a quiet place to study. They also argue that students miss the social side of school — talking to friends, working in teams and asking questions face to face. Many experts now believe that the best approach is a mix of both: online materials for practice and classroom time for discussion and cooperation.
questions.text: What is one advantage of online learning mentioned in the text?
options: Students can study at their own speed.
